title: When two methods become one study
source: Johnson, Onwuegbuzie & Turner · Journal of Mixed Methods Research · 2007

cues.text: A survey tells you how common an experience is. Interviews can help explain how people live it.
When should bringing those approaches together count as mixed methods research?
The three authors invited thirty-six methodologists. They analyzed nineteen definitions, some written jointly.
They compared them systematically to identify recurring ideas.
The definitions differed on what gets mixed, when or where it happens, and how broad the mixing is.
They also differed on why researchers mix, and on the philosophical or practical orientation that guides their work.
A mixed study can be mainly qualitative, give the two strands equal status, or be mainly quantitative.
The lead strand reflects the purpose and design of the study.
The authors' general definition combines elements of qualitative and quantitative approaches.
That combination can broaden what we see, deepen what we understand, and help us check whether findings support each other.
The authors argue for mixed methods as a third paradigm. Their tentative fuller definition adds pragmatism and social awareness.
The invited group offers a starting point. Researchers still have to explain why their particular combination makes sense.
